rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-wāqiʿa may modify an omitted Resurrection or earthquake.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون الواقعة صفة لمحذوف وهي القيامة أو الزلزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the omitted noun is an unspecified event, with the feminine ending signaling its gravity and terror.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المحذوف شيئا غير معين ، وتكون تاء التأنيث مشيرة إلى شدة الأمر الواقع وهوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic wording of al-wāqiʿa conveys an event exceeding the bare fact that something happened, as in kānat al-kāʾina.
rows.anchor: كانت الكائنة والمراد كان الأمر كائنا ما كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like rāwiya and nassāba, a final hāʾ can compress an added intensive description into one letter; here the intensification is semantic, despite feminine agreement in the verb.
rows.anchor: نأتي بحرف نيابة عن كلمة كما أتينا بهاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes a preceding verb, اذكر, govern idhā as an object rather than a temporal adverb.
rows.anchor: فعل متقدم يجعل إذا مفعولا به لا ظرفا وهو اذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second analysis makes laysa liwaqʿatihā kādhiba the governor of idhā.
rows.anchor: العامل فيها ليس لوقعتها كاذبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third analysis supplies the day when people are lowered and raised, indicated by khāfiḍa rāfiʿa.
rows.anchor: يخفض قوم ويرفع قوم ، وقد دل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed governor is the statement about the people of the right, understood as occurring on the day the Event occurs.
rows.anchor: أي في يوم وقوع الواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-waqʿa signals a single occurrence: the event happens all at once, one time.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أنها تقع دفعة واحدة فالوقعة للمرة الواحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kādhiba may be an adjective for an omitted person or soul: no soul lies about its occurrence.
rows.anchor: كاذبة صفة لمحذوف أقيمت مقامه تقديره ليس لها نفس تكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine ending may instead intensify the noun, by the same account given for al-wāqiʿa.
rows.anchor: الهاء للمبالغة كما تقول في الواقعة وقد تقدم بيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kādhiba may be a verbal noun, like al-ʿāqiba.
rows.anchor: هي مصدر كالعاقبة فإن قلنا بالوجه الأول فاللام تحتمل وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the lām causal, no one lies that day because its occurrence is so overwhelming; the denial is general.
rows.anchor: لا تكذب نفس في ذلك اليوم لشدة وقعتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal reading can also mean that no one can falsely claim there is no Resurrection, though people had denied it before.
rows.anchor: لا يكذب أحد فيقول : لا قيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the lām marks an object or relation, the sense is that no person can be found falsifying the Event when reporting it.
rows.anchor: وذلك كما يقال : ليس لزيد ضارب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom also rebukes someone who assumes a great undertaking is easy: the Event cannot be made easy by that claim.
rows.anchor: ليس لها كاذب يقول : هي أمر سهل يطاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the intensive reading, no great liar can lie then, because the day's terror prevents it.
rows.anchor: ليس لها كاذب عظيم بمعنى أن من يكذب ويقدم على الكذب العظيم لا يمكنه أن يكذب لهول ذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, anyone denying the Event then would be an immense liar; Rāzī says the previous reading better conveys the day's terror.
rows.anchor: أن أحدا لو كذب وقال في ذلك اليوم لا قيامة ولا واقعة لكان كاذبا عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first intensive interpretation better expresses the horror of the Day.
rows.anchor: والأول أدل على هول اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If kādhiba is a verbal noun, the verse means no one lies about the Day and everyone affirms it.
rows.anchor: يعود ما ذكرنا إلى أنه لا كاذب في ذلك اليوم بل كل أحد يصدقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāfiḍa and rāfiʿa may modify the implied person or soul who does not lie or alter speech.
rows.anchor: خافضة رافعة صفتان للنفس الكاذبة أي ليس لوقعتها من يكذب ولا من يغير الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired denial excludes even slight distortion, extending from a false statement to false qualifications and incidental details.
rows.anchor: وهذا لأن الكاذب قد يكذب في حقيقة الأمر وربما يكذب في صفة صفاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing coordinates the first al-sābiqūn with the people of the right; the following clause then says those are the brought near.
rows.anchor: والسابقون } عطف على { وأصحاب * الميمنة } ( الواقعة : 8 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition can mark the subject's renown, so no predicate is needed; Rāzī cites a poet's line أنا أبو النجم وشعري شعري as an example.
rows.anchor: شهرة أمر المبتدأ بما هو عليه فلا حاجة إلى الخبر عنه وهو مراد الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, repetition says their condition surpasses human knowledge, like being able to describe a king only as a king.
rows.anchor: أن في المبتدأ مالا يحيط العلم به ولا يخبر عنه ولا يعرف منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the question about the people of the right, the forerunners are not challenged to explain themselves because they already admit human inability to grasp their state.
rows.anchor: الاستفهام الذي للإعجاز يورد على مدعي العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers the repeated-subject reading as the most balanced and sound explanation.
rows.anchor: والوجه الأوسط هو الأعدل الأصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is that those who race to good works in this life will be the first to Paradise in the next.
rows.anchor: أن المراد منه أن السابقين إلى الخيرات في الدنيا هم السابقون إلى الجنة في العقبى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third parsing treats the second al-sābiqūn as an emphatic repetition of the first.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : هو أن السابقون ثانيا تأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restriction applies among the three human groups: the forerunners reach the highest degree of nearness, while other groups may also be near at lower, unbounded degrees; angels can be called near as well.
rows.anchor: أولئك المقربون } يقتضي الحصر فينبغي أن لا يكون غيرهم مقربا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation places the forerunners near the gardens while the people of the right are still heading there and receiving their books after an easy reckoning.
rows.anchor: المراد السابقون مقربون من الجنات حال كون أصحاب اليمين متوجهين إلى طريق الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation makes their nearness to God in Paradise a continuing ascent: as others approach, the forerunners rise further, reaching the highest levels as the others reach the houris.
rows.anchor: قربهم إلى الله في الجنة وأصحاب اليمين بعد متوجهون إلى ما وصل إليه المقربون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse first names those affected by the warnings, then explains the forerunners before the people of the left because the forerunners' merit deserves priority in this exposition.
rows.anchor: عند البيان فذكر السابق لفضيلته وفضيلة حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath's object may be the Qur'an, which opponents called poetry or magic.
rows.anchor: القرآن كانوا يجعلونه تارة شعرا وأخرى سحرا وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more apparent object is monotheism and resurrection.
rows.anchor: هو التوحيد والحشر وهو أظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reads lā uqsim as not declining to swear because the matter is plain or the oath insignificant; it is a great oath, and God swears by something greater because the truth is certain.
rows.anchor: وكان معناه : لا أقسم بهذا لوضوح المقسم به عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human oaths are called intensified because of their grave sin, but God's oath is called great: its nonphysical greatness reaches many hearts and fills them with awe, by analogy with a large body filling space.
rows.anchor: اليمين في أكثر الأمر توصف بالمغلظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the already known revelation sent to Muhammad, which people called poetry or magic.
rows.anchor: إلى معلوم وهو الكلام الذي أنزل على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it refers to the preceding sura's discourse on monotheism, resurrection, their proofs, and the oath, which opponents called Muhammad's invention.
rows.anchor: إلى مذكور وهو جميع ما سبق في سورة الواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾān may be a verbal noun used for its object, the recited text; Rāzī compares this usage to 13:31 and 31:11.
rows.anchor: مصدر أريد به المفعول وهو المقروء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Qurʾān is a noun for what is recited, like qurbān for what one offers devotionally and ḥulwān for what is given or tasted.
rows.anchor: اسم لما يقرأ كالقربان لما يتقرب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This noun reading answers critics of jurists' zakat term al-jubrān: it can name the thing by which compensation is made, like Qurʾān names what is recited.
rows.anchor: هو اسم لما يجبر به كالقربان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer is that opponents rejected the whole description Qurʾān noble, not merely the fact that the text could be recited.
rows.anchor: فهم كانوا ينكرون كونه قرآنا كريما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers that opponents called it invented: calling it a Qurʾān establishes that Muhammad received and recited it, and that it will be recited forever in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: أثبت كونه مقروءا على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ليقرأ ويتلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike ordinary speech that grows stale through repetition, the Qurʾān remains fresh forever; even angels who knew it long before Muhammad hear it with a new listener's delight.
rows.anchor: لا يهون بكثرة التلاوة ويبقى أبد الدهر كالكلام الغض والحديث الطري

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported definition of karīm is something pure in origin and manifest in excellence; lineage or character alone does not capture the full sense.
rows.anchor: قيل : الكريم هو الذي كان طاهر الأصل ظاهر الفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Common usage narrows karam to easy or abundant giving because people prize what they receive; Rāzī calls this a bad custom and defines true nobility by purity of origin and evident excellence.
rows.anchor: الكريم هو الذي استجمع فيه ما ينبغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān is noble in its pure source, manifest virtue, eloquent wording, and sound meaning.
rows.anchor: فالقرآن أيضا كريم بمعنى طاهر الأصل ظاهر الفضل لفظه فصيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary usage too, the Qurʾān gives each seeker what they need: jurists, sages, and writers draw on it, and its wording is unusually easy to memorize and preserve exactly.
rows.anchor: فالفقيه يستدل به ويأخذ منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As ʿazīz, the Qurʾān leaves those who turn away with nothing, unlike other books whose meanings may remain after they are forgotten.
rows.anchor: ولكونه عزيزا أن كل من يعرض عنه لا يبقى معه منه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As ḥakīm, it makes those who engage with it wholeheartedly independent of other sciences.
rows.anchor: ولكونه حكيما من اشتغل به وأقبل عليه بالقلب أغناه عن سائر العلوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the Qurʾān itself as being in a book, namely the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: فكذلك ههنا أن القرآن كريم وهو في كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A related reading takes noble as its quality in the book: the Qurʾān is noble in the Preserved Tablet even if disbelievers do not regard it as noble.
rows.anchor: فالقرآن كريم في اللوح المحفوظ وإن لم يكن كريما عند الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes the whole description Qurʾān noble the content written in the book, as in the statement about ʿIlliyyūn.
rows.anchor: والمراد حينئذ أنه في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All these readings are sound, but the first most strongly honors the heavenly recited text.
rows.anchor: والأول أبلغ في التعظيم بالمقروء السماوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is most correctly identified as the Preserved Tablet, supported by 85:21–22.
rows.anchor: وهو الأصح أنه اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view identifies the book as the codex.
rows.anchor: الثاني : الكتاب هو المصحف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies it as an earlier revealed scripture, so the Qurʾān is also found in the Torah, Gospel, and other scriptures.
rows.anchor: كتاب من الكتب المنزلة فهو قرآن في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the word's pattern raises an objection, a tablet whose function is to receive writing can itself be called a book, as with words for a covering or a storage chest.
rows.anchor: اللوح لما لم يكن إلا الذي يكتب فيه صح تسميته كتابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maknūn means perfectly protected; concealment is the attendant of the highest protection, since what is precious is hidden from sight.
rows.anchor: كلما تزداد عزته يزداد ستره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the Tablet is literally hidden from sight except for selected angels, while the written Qurʾān is protected from alteration and corrupting hands.
rows.anchor: اللوح المحفوظ مستور عن العين لا يطلع عليه إلا ملائكة مخصوصون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book answers those who said the recitation came from jinn: the angel received it from a book before delivering it, so it is not even angelic speech, much less jinn speech.
rows.anchor: لم ينزل به عليه الملك إلا بعدما أخذه من كتاب فهو ليس بكلام الملائكة فضلا أن يكون كلام الجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maknūn answers the claim that it is ancient lore in open books: it is concealed, and only the purified touch it.
rows.anchor: لا بل هو { في كتاب مكنون * لا يمسه إلا المطهرون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it a Qurʾān rebuts the claim that Muhammad composed it himself.
rows.anchor: أن وصفه بكونه قرآنا صار ردا على من قال

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī forbids both the person with minor impurity and the sexually impure person from touching the codex, but bars only the latter from reciting the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: الشافعي رحمه الله منع المحدث والجنب من مس المصحف وجعلهما غير مطهرين ثم منع الجنب عن قراءة القرآن ولم يمنع المحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reasons that the sexually impure person is unfit for Qurʾānic remembrance because 4:43 bars him from the mosque, whereas 24:36 authorizes entry for those admitted to remembrance.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو كان أهلا للذكر لما منعه من دخول المسجد لأنه تعالى أذن لأهل الذكر في الدخول

rows.speaker: الصحابة
rows.claim: Rāzī cites that some Companions entered the mosque while in minor impurity as evidence that such a person is not barred from it.
rows.anchor: فإن من الصحابة من كان يدخل المسجد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet permitted people to sleep in the mosque; Rāzī uses this to show that minor impurity does not by itself bar entry.
rows.anchor: وجوز النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم نوم القوم في المسجد وليس النوم حدثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep itself is not a state of impurity, though particular sleep may legally entail it, with disagreement among jurists.
rows.anchor: إذ النوم الخاص يلزمه الحكم بالحدث على اختلاف بين الأئمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī calls the Qurʾān absolute remembrance, citing 43:44; he reads mosque remembrance in 24:36 to include Qurʾānic recitation, the required remembrance in prayer.
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى : { وإنه لذكر لك ولقومك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other formulas may be ordinary statements or remembrance depending on intent, but Qurʾān is remembrance by its form; saying it as a report or order makes one no longer a reciter, though the words remain Qurʾān, and invalidates prayer.
rows.anchor: يخرج عن كونه قارئا للقرآن
